o1.biggest_strength: It catches the in-app checkout bug as a ship-now fix, sizes the upside correctly, and builds the test plan around the actual data signals rather than generic CRO ideas.
o1.biggest_mistake: The schedule suggests overlapping tests while saying each gets all traffic, which needs a clear factorial setup or it could muddy the read on mobile.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Clarify the test sequencing/factorial design and update baselines after the checkout fix before launch.

o2.biggest_strength: It is very clear, calls out the broken in-app checkout first, and gives honest math for what two-week tests can detect on add-to-cart.
o2.biggest_mistake: It leans too hard on add-to-cart as the main metric for all five tests, so a winner could be shipped while the order impact is still too weakly read.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Use order conversion as the main metric where the change is meant to drive buying confidence, add longer run times or larger MDEs for those tests, and include the reviews/tracking ship-now items.

reason: Both are usable, but Output 1 is the plan I would rather hand to the team: it sizes the bug upside, ships the right low-risk fixes, and gives a fuller order-focused test plan tied to the data. Output 2 is cleaner to read, but its two-week add-to-cart framing is less safe for conversion decisions.
